deep_why: The method retrieves instructions and interface diagrams by computing relevance between user text and both captions of pictures plus transcripts of videos. It works because combining two independent retrieval paths—one searching descriptions directly, another finding documentation passages then pulling their linked images and video clips—gives richer coverage than either alone. When a user asks how to perform a task, direct image search catches cases where the interface itself answers the question, while text-guided expansion catches cases where the concept lives in written docs with linked visuals. The two signals are complementary: text might mismatch visually complex steps, but images of those exact steps will show the interface details that matter. Together they capture both semantic meaning and procedural visuals, delivering more complete and actionable responses.

Revenue metrics in A/B tests are often dominated by a tiny fraction of high-spending users, so their random ups and downs dominate measurement noise, drowning signal in variance. The method groups users by pre-experiment spending patterns and adjusts results within each group before pooling, which works because within-group variance is much lower than overall variance. The principle is that stratification isolates true differences from noise: if a small group of whales happened to spend more this week by random chance, stratifying controls for that coincidence. Combining this with covariate adjustment further removes predictable variation using historical data. Since noise is what wastes traffic in underpowered experiments, reducing it means the same sample size detects smaller true effects, so equal sensitivity requires fewer users.

Fresh items with no engagement history are invisible to collaborative-filtering systems, which learn only from past signals. The method solves this by embedding items into a learned hierarchical code (semantic ID) built from residual quantization—stacking codes from coarse to fine—so new items sharing the same coarse prefixes as popular old items inherit relevance signals. This works because the hierarchy naturally generalizes: even if an item is brand new, its coarse topic code connects it to thousands of seen items, so the system can estimate engagement before any clicks. The framework additionally aligns these semantic codes with a query-item ranking model and uses both content descriptions and user-engagement patterns to guide learning. This joint alignment works because semantic structure and engagement patterns inform each other: if items with similar codes get similar engagement, the structure captures meaningful user preferences, making the codes reliable for ranking.

Short-video platforms face a conflict: showing the highest-engagement videos maximizes immediate user satisfaction but starves new creators of visibility, shrinking content supply long-term. The method frames this as a constrained optimization: maximize user satisfaction subject to minimum exposure constraints for creators at critical growth stages. This works because constrained optimization formalizes the trade-off mathematically, guaranteeing both objectives are honored—not one at the expense of the other. The primal-dual solution method decouples global creator-exposure targets into per-request decisions in real time by tracking how close the system is to exposure quotas and adjusting recommendations accordingly. The guarantee holds because the algorithm maintains a dual variable that rises when constraints are violated, penalizing violations until the system complies, so exposure targets become binding without requiring global coordination at ranking time.

Fashion compatibility rules are contextual—a sofa matches one table but not another depending on style, era, or material—so rigid category-specific rules fail. The method treats compatibility as a conditional retrieval task where textual style descriptors (like 'mid-century modern' or 'oak') dynamically select which visual features matter. This works because text encodes style rules that are impossible to learn from pixel statistics alone. By fusing text and image through attention—allowing text to gate which visual features activate—the model learns that 'modern' style should attend to clean lines while 'classic' should attend to ornamental details. Training on triplet comparisons (compatible pairs vs. incompatible pairs with shared categories) directly enforces that the same category pair can be compatible or incompatible depending on style, so the model learns to condition predictions on textual context. This joint conditioning reveals that many failures of image-only systems stem from missing the semantic rules that govern what 'goes together.'

E-commerce marketplaces receive millions of products daily against thousands of policies, making exhaustive checking computationally infeasible. The method uses a learned retrieval stage that identifies which handful of policies each new product might violate, acting as a fast filter before slower manual review. This works because most products violate only a few policies, so a high-recall router can eliminate obvious cases cheaply, letting reviewers focus effort on borderline items. The system encodes complex policy text into description vectors that are aligned with product images (through CLIP), so relevance matching between policies and products runs quickly via vector similarity. Including hard negatives in training—products that are visually similar to policy violations but actually compliant—forces the system to learn fine-grained distinctions, improving precision. This architecture is sound because a retrieval filter that catches the vast majority of problematic products while letting few false negatives slip through dramatically reduces verification cost without sacrificing safety.

Aligning large language models to produce factually correct table answers requires feedback, but simple preference pairs (answer A is better than B) hide why A works—whether it got the SQL right, chose the right column, or reasoned about filters correctly. The method augments preferences with explanations of the reasoning that makes one answer correct, then trains the model to learn from both the preference and the explanation. This works because reasoning traces ground the learning signal: if the model learns that 'filtering by date range' or 'summing the revenue column' leads to correctness, it internalizes the reasoning patterns that generalize beyond the specific examples. Unlike binary preferences that only signal which answer is better, reason-augmented feedback teaches the underlying rules. Applied to structured data queries, this means the model learns which query semantics (joins, aggregations, filters) actually correspond to correct table logic, not just which output looks better in isolation.

A user's immediate intent (what they want to do now) is shaped by what they plan to do next—a customer asking for a product refund likely intends to revisit feedback first. Standard methods infer intent only from past actions, missing this forward-looking structure. The method predicts the next action the user will take, then uses that prediction to guide the main intent model. This works because next actions carry information: if the model learns that users heading toward complaint submission show distinct behavior patterns, predicting those patterns helps identify intent signals that raw history alone misses. The framework trains both forward prediction and intent classification jointly, with the prediction acting as auxiliary training that forces the model to learn representations capturing the full behavioral arc. This dual training works because it exploits causality: next behavior doesn't cause current intent, but both flow from the same underlying user goal, so conditioning on next behavior serves as a learned sensor for that latent goal.

E-commerce platforms in emerging markets often lack structured product attributes, making faceted search and ranking difficult. The method uses a language model to propose attributes for each category, then iteratively improves them through developer review and human annotation feedback. This works because language models can infer reasonable attributes from product names and category context, and human feedback closes the loop: annotators catch errors, spurring prompt refinement that produces better proposals next round. Structured iteration matters because each error pattern in early proposals is visible to humans, who can guide the language model toward the domain conventions that matter locally—sizes matter for clothing, materials for furniture. Once attributes are tagged on products, they enable three improvements: filtering now becomes granular, ranking models gain structured features, and text representations become semantically richer. The method is sound because it trades human time for automated generation, amplifying that human effort through iterative refinement rather than requiring experts to build taxonomies from scratch.

Vision-language models are often evaluated on general tasks, but fashion e-commerce requires extracting style attributes, color, fit, and material—tasks where performance varies wildly across models and models behave inconsistently across prompts. The paper measures this variation systematically across six commercial and two open-source models on five fashion-specific tasks. This matters because a model performing best on general vision-language benchmarks might perform worse on extracting fit or fabric, and its strengths and weaknesses are model-specific not prompt-specific, meaning organizations cannot simply tune prompts to fix problems. Continuous monitoring reveals that model updates improve some capabilities while degrading others, so organizations relying on models need ongoing evaluation in their specific domain. The benchmark's value lies in exposing the mismatch between general-purpose performance and operational reality: what works across diverse internet images may fail on the specific structured extraction tasks that drive e-commerce systems.

Search results are relevant but undermonetized, so platforms want to boost high-revenue products. Reranking all results to maximize revenue alone would degrade relevance and user trust, so the problem becomes: select a reordering that maximizes revenue while keeping relevance and fraud-risk above thresholds. The method formulates this as an optimization problem, then solves it approximately by repeatedly swapping adjacent items if the swap improves revenue or fixes a violated constraint. This works because swapping neighbors is fast and the algorithm terminates when no productive swaps remain, giving a locally optimal ordering within deployment latency limits. The principle underlying this approximation is that many constraints are 'loose'—slightly violated swaps can fix them without large revenue loss—so local search finds solutions that honor constraints and capture a large fraction of the ideal revenue. The approach is practical because it avoids solving an expensive exact optimization for every query, yet maintains all constraints, proving that constrained reranking can coexist with relevance.

Recommending short videos by predicting which items users will click from their entire watch history requires modeling sequences of hundreds or thousands of items, but transformer attention is quadratic in sequence length, making ultra-long histories computationally infeasible. The method addresses representation first: instead of orthogonal video IDs (which are arbitrary and demand embedding tables as large as the item catalog), the system learns hierarchical semantic IDs from actual video content. This shrinks the embedding space dramatically. Second, to handle sequence length, the method compresses sequences using temporal folding—grouping nearby videos and keeping only key representatives—plus a global query that captures long-range dependencies outside the main attention. This works because video sequences are redundant: users watching ten similar content in a row contain information mostly in the first few; folding loses little while cutting compute quadratically. Global queries capture information from older, less recent content without attending to every item. Together, semantic representation and compression reduce memory from proportional to catalog size and quadratic in history length to practical levels for billion-user deployment.

Two-tower recommendation systems split the model into user and item branches to enable fast serving—the user tower runs once per query, the item tower precomputes all items. This efficiency cost decoupling prevents fine-grained user-item interactions that ranking models exploit. The method trains a user tower with guidance from the target item, learning to align user representations with what that specific item needs, then at serving time discards the item-specific information and uses only the pre-computed user representation. This works because training creates a smarter user representation that captures item-specific nuances even after the item signal is removed. Three components drive this: first, user-item semantic alignment through contrastive learning teaches the tower to foreground signals relevant to the target; second, modeling multiple user interests as a discrete space (via vector quantization) captures heterogeneous preferences explicitly; third, adaptively fusing target-aware interests at multiple levels reconstructs fine-grained signals from coarse tower outputs. The trick is that guidance during training leaves permanent improvements in the learned representation, so decoupling at inference incurs no serving cost.

Novelty recommendation balances relevance (user wants it) against diversity (content is different from recent watches), which are inherently opposed: the most relevant item is often what they just watched. Large language models can generate coherent lists by reasoning about intent and diversity together, but industrial deployment needs: (1) supervision on what 'novel' means, and (2) learning to balance relevance and diversity at both the sequence level (overall coherence) and item level (individual redundancy). The method synthesizes training data by combining user logs with generated rationales, creating high-quality examples of why an item is novel. For optimization, it uses hierarchical reasoning—a novelty tag guides search direction, an interest topic refines intent, and list construction happens in stages. A two-level reward optimization (sequence and item objectives) prevents the classical pitfall where maximizing overall list quality still allows redundant items. This hierarchy works because it structures the reasoning in human-like stages: humans first think 'what should we explore,' then 'what specifically,' then 'what order matters,' and item-level rewards enforce non-redundancy at the execution stage.

Predicting post-click conversion rates is hard because discount rates strongly influence purchase likelihood—cheaper items convert more—but discount distributions are skewed (most items get no discount, a few get heavy discounts) and promotions vary seasonally, creating complex non-linearities. The method extracts frequency components of item discount rates using Fourier transform, which works because many natural patterns (trend, seasonality, repetition) are periodic, and frequency decomposition reveals these periodicities cleanly. Removing seasonal and user-specific biases separately addresses the core issue that a user's discount sensitivity depends on what other items they saw: someone accustomed to discounts behaves differently from someone seeing their first sale. The auxiliary regression task that predicts item discount rates forces the model to learn a refined representation of discount magnitude, making the representation more informative for conversion. Together, these components work because discount influence is not random noise—it has structure (periodicity, user-specificity, item-specificity)—and the model explicitly learns to measure and condition on that structure rather than treating discount as a black-box covariate.
